mentions.text: We are really terrible at predicting what's easy and what's hard -- 15 years ago we were screaming at truck drivers to learn to code, lol. Another really fun story I like -- what if in the summer of 2020 (GPT-3 release) someone told you that language model was about as close to self-driving as Tesla's Autopilot was, with it's billions of miles of data and vision-first approach. Would have sounded nutty, but VLAs drive cars now. My lack of surprisal is mostly appreciating the uncertainty in dealing with unknowns. But I generally agree, there's a lot of takes now about "RH fell, cancer is next", and I'm very skeptical. We'll probably see lots of progress in parts of biology or physics that already have ready-made verification systems, there's probably lots of business opportunities in building physical verifiers, and there's probably a lot potential in applying existing methods to larger data sets like the Vera Rubin telescope. But what if you need a 50B telescope and 20 years to build it in order to verify some physics hypothesis? What if you do need a RCT across a population to verify a new drug hypothesis? Progress will look a lot like classical progress then, despite AI.

mentions.text: If the LLM (Grok bot and CLI) I use didn't work for me, or wasted tokens without me being able to tell it to optimize how it works successfully, I wouldn't be using it. They have to tread carefully because local LLM models are going to take over here shortly, so the longer they can hold onto subscribers the better for them. This all points to Local LLM's being more than capable and optimizations + RAM production are going to accelerate that in the next 1-5 years. Right now "workstations" are $99-$120k each, but remember the 90's when graphics workstations were that much, and then they hit $3k or less in just a short few years? The same thing is going to happen for AI computers at home, and models on them, within the same period of time.

mentions.text: This is extremely common, and even as someone who frequently discusses the "AI bubble", this doesn't mean a heck of a lot. There are a lot of structural forces that apply to a newly IPO'd stock both formal (various lockup periods ending and supply coming online, Anthropic's schedule of this is particularly complicated) and informal (that day one pop is manufactured by design). You'll find if you try to trade on this general pattern that you've mostly been beaten to it; the options will have this pattern already priced in, you won't be able to borrow stock to short for any reasonable price, etc. The only thing you can really do is understand that day one may not be the best day to get in, in general, for any IPO. I popped the question into my friendly neighborhood AI as to whether there have been any major IPOs where the IPO price ended up serving as the floor for the stock, and it's a short list, though with some major names in it. Microsoft (1986), Nvidia (1999), Google (2004), Visa (2008), and in the 2020s, Airbnb, Snowflake, Zoom (2019, though arguably helped a lot by a Certain Event), Reddit, and more-or-less Arm. Amazon and Tesla are near-misses. But there's been a lot of IPOs
